body: The tinfoil has moved. A woman who came into the supermarket for tinfoil in the second week of October is standing in the middle aisle where it used to be, in front of a pallet of tins in a red sleeve, a tower of selection boxes, and a cardboard reindeer at knee height that a child in front of her is already touching. She is not offended by any of it. She notices, mildly, that it is early, then finds the tinfoil two aisles down and does not think about it again. By the second week of December she will have thought about very little else.

Nobody delivered a teaching to her in that aisle. She was simply told, by the arrangement of a room, what the next ten weeks were going to be about. She agreed to none of it and she will keep all of it.

The usual objection to the feasts is that they belong to somebody else — that they are cultural rather than binding, and that keeping them is either sentimental or a quiet walk back into law. It is a serious objection and it deserves a serious answer. It also assumes something it never states.

The assumption is that the alternative is no calendar at all — that a person who does not keep the feasts is going about their year unshaped, free to think about whatever occurs to them next. There is no such person. Everyone lives inside a year with a shape, and the shape is doing something. It decides when you feel behind, when you feel generous, when you are expected to be happy and when you are permitted to rest. It arrives in shop layouts, in what the radio plays in November, in the week the school term breaks. Nobody signed up for it, and nobody escapes it by disapproving of it, which is the part that catches the people most confident they have.

One of those two years was written down in advance, with the order given and the reasons attached. The other was assembled by people who never announced it and cannot be asked about it. Both run to a schedule. Only one published its schedule — which is also how this dial works: fixed numbers, 121 stations, the programme posted before it airs.

Keeping a different year costs something, and the cost is social rather than theological. It means being out of step in small, repeated, faintly awkward ways: explaining to colleagues why you want those particular days off, being the household not doing the thing everybody else is doing that week, and doing it annually, in front of people who find it eccentric. That is a real price, paid in small change rather than one large sum. It is paid because a calendar is a curriculum. It decides what you think about, in what order, every year, whether or not you agreed to it.

The retail year is not a conspiracy and nobody in particular is running it. It is simply what happens when a year gets optimised and nothing about it is promised. A long build to December, a slump, a manufactured romance in February, a summer, a return to school, and round again. Read that curriculum honestly and it teaches acquisition, then exhaustion, then acquisition. It teaches it to everybody at the same time, every year, including the people who would tell you they are not participating — because the aisle does not check whether you approve before it rearranges itself around you.

The feast cycle is arranged differently, and the arrangement is most of the teaching. It is agricultural before it is anything else, tied to a barley harvest, a wheat harvest, an ingathering, so the year is anchored to things that happen outside rather than to a shopping season. It moves through deliverance, provision, harvest, atonement and dwelling, in an order that repeats. A household inside it learns the sequence the way a child learns a route — not by studying it, but by having been taken along it enough times.
So the question was never whether to keep a calendar. The question is whose, and what it is teaching while nobody is watching.

Take the objection seriously for a moment, because it earns it. A person can keep the feasts badly. They can be kept as costume, or as a way of feeling more authentic than the congregation down the road, or as a ledger — days observed, boxes ticked, a quiet confidence accumulating. That failure is real and not rare, and anybody who has been near these circles for long has met it. But it is a failure of the person, not of the year. The retail calendar produces its own devotees and nobody argues from that to abolishing December. A curriculum is not discredited by a bad student.
Everyone is enrolled somewhere. The only choice is where.

A man puts up a shelter in a small back garden in the first week of autumn, out of two lengths of batten, a tarpaulin, and branches from a neighbour’s hedge that the neighbour was glad to be rid of. It is not a good shelter. It leaks on the second night, and his youngest refuses to sleep in it and goes to her own bed like a sensible person. They eat out there four evenings running with coats on. His eldest, eleven, who has spent most of the year finding her parents embarrassing, asks on the third evening why they do this, and he gives an answer that is not very well put, and she accepts it and goes back to her plate.

She will not remember the answer. She will remember that for one week every autumn the family ate outside in the cold on purpose, that there was a reason for it, and that the reason was older than her father.

Here is the part that is not tidy. Keeping a calendar does not make a year good. There are households that keep every appointed day and are miserable inside them, and there are believers who keep none of them and are plainly further along than I am. The feasts are not a lever. Anybody who tells you a life will come right once the dates are right is selling something, and what is usually being sold is a sense of superiority over the church down the road.

But that concession does not hand us back the neutral year, because the neutral year does not exist. A curriculum that shapes nobody is still a curriculum. It simply teaches whatever it teaches to people who are not attending. The feast cycle is not offered here as a guarantee of anything. It is offered as a better syllabus than the one most people are enrolled in by default, running to a schedule that was published rather than arranged quietly behind them.

So the feasts are not nostalgia, whatever else may be true of them. They are a year with a stated order and stated reasons, tied to harvests and to events, repeating until the sequence lives in a household rather than in a book. Set against a year that teaches acquisition and exhaustion and never once explains itself, that is not a sentimental preference. It is a plain comparison of two curricula, and only one of them is willing to say what it is for.
All of which is theory until a year has to be lived a week at a time. So here is the part that is not theory.

A calendar is kept in a house by what the house does, and a great deal of what a house does is set by what is playing in it. That is the plainest place to start. The dial carries 121 stations across a band running from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70: music mostly, some teaching and prayer, family programming safe to leave on with children in the room, and 40 frequencies for the nations in their own languages. Every station holds its number permanently, which rhymes with the argument above — a frequency, like an appointed day, is in the same place every time you go looking for it.

Start at HM 306.20 — Hebraic Celebrations. It is the messianic worship frequency, and it belongs at the end of this argument because it is the one station built around the appointed times rather than around a release schedule. It carries the songs a household actually needs in order to keep a year: the ones for a table, for a spring evening, for the week the shelter goes up in the garden. That is the practical difficulty most families hit — not the theology, which they have read a good deal about, but arriving at the evening itself with nothing to sing and a sense that something ought to be happening. This frequency answers that problem, and it is running now, whether or not today is a feast.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else there. And do make yourself an account while you are at it. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how the band learns which frequencies households are reaching for and when — which is how the next one gets built.

So do not study it. Studying is what people do with the feasts instead of keeping them, and it can go on comfortably for years. Put HM 306.20 on this evening while the table is being laid, and let a household hear the shape of a different year before anybody has to be persuaded of it. That is how a calendar gets into a family in any case: not by argument, but by having been in the room often enough that the children assume it was always there.
